newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai cargo picks up after Ramadan but rates stick.
newsitem.headline: Dubai cargo picks up after Ramadan but rates stick.

text.p: Air freight business out of Dubai has started to pick up slowly after more than a month of subdued trade during a Moslem fasting period, but industry executives say there is little sign of rates increasing any time soon.

"The market is very good. We are chock-a-block and have the opportunity to be more selective," said an upbeat Dubai cargo sales manager at a large European carrier. "But rates have been stable for the past two months."
"It is not a boom period, nor is it lean. Business is okay, particularly since the Eid (Moslem holiday in mid-February), when it was very quiet," said a forwarder.
Another agent said: "Dubai is not doing well at all, but rates are looking okay. Hopefully March will be better."
While opinions differ widely amongst agents and airlines, the consensus is that things could always be better in the Dubai air freight industry. They say the figures speak for themselves.

Airport statistics show that February was indeed a quieter month, with Dubai cargo traffic falling 2.64 percent to 28,165 tonnes, dragged down by a seven percent year-on-year fall in exports to 12,765 tonnes. Meanwhile, volumes in nearby Sharjah rose 26 percent in February to 28,565 tonnes.

"Sharjah is moving up. Airlines with offices in the Dubai Cargo Village are carrying out more and more business through Sharjah and Abu Dhabi," said one analyst, adding that preferential rates are making the UAE's two other major airports Operators say orders and shipments held up by the Ramadan fasting month and the Chinese New Year are now filtering through to the market, signalling more business ahead. But excess capacity is likely to keep the lid on any major rate increases.
"The traffic and orders delayed during Ramadan are now moving out. Europe is getting into full swing again, so things are better," said one.
They say European business is gradually moving back to normal after the usual post-Christmas lull with orders set to drive more air freight traffic through the emirate.

One executive said since the end of the Chinese New Year -- when business in the Far East comes to a virtual standstill -- aircraft transiting Dubai from the Far East are carrying heavier loads to Europe: "There is less capacity to sell, but rates haven't moved up."
He said, however, that this gave some airlines the opportunity to be more selective about what they carried.

A Reuters survey shows that the average rate on a 100 kg shipment with a six-to-one volume-to-weight ratio to London Heathrow is two fils firmer than its mid-Ramadan level, at 4.07 dirhams. The same applies for Frankfurt.
Many major carriers are charging a simple $1(3.67 dirham) fee per kg to Heathrow and Frankfurt, while certain forwarders still quote rates as high as 5.40 on small volume shipments.

Business to the U.S. keeps ticking over, with textile shipments starting to trickle through. Rates are unchanged, with Reuters calculations putting the average to JKF at 6.45 and the rate to Los Angeles at an average 7.50 dirhams.
Agents said movements to Africa continued to be strong, with rates to Nairobi hovering around an established 4.15. To Entebbe, tariffs are slightly higher at 4.75 dirhams.

"More African traders have been coming since the end of Ramadan. They buy all sorts of goods here to sell at home and send them back as personal effects," said a forwarder active in the East Africa market.
Air shipments to the Far East remain steady at 4.00 dirhams a kg to both Singapore and Hong Kong.
